frames.narration: A three-tier app over 3 availability zones needs 3 x 3 = 9 subnets. The architect picks the private range 10.20.0.0/16: the first 16 bits are the network, the other 16 give 2^16 = 65,536 addresses.

Before building anything, check for overlap. On-prem already uses 10.0.0.0/16. 10.20.0.0/16 starts at a different second byte, so the ranges do not overlap and a VPN is possible. Had we picked 10.0.0.0/16, a packet for 10.0.5.9 would be ambiguous.

Nine subnets need ceil(log2 9) = 4 extra bits, so the /16 is cut into 16 slots of /20. Each /20 has 2^12 = 4,096 addresses, of which 4,091 are usable (5 are reserved). 9 slots are used and 7 stay free.

Each tier gets three consecutive /20s, one per zone: public 10.20.0.0, .16.0 and .32.0; private (app) 10.20.48.0, .64.0 and .80.0; database 10.20.96.0, .112.0 and .128.0. Subnet 10.20.48.0/20 spans 10.20.48.0 to 10.20.63.255, and its first usable address is 10.20.48.4.
Route tables decide where packets go. The private subnets get three routes: 10.20.0.0/16 to local, 10.0.0.0/16 to the VPN, and 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway.

An app server at 10.20.48.10 sends a request to the on-prem host 10.0.0.5. Two routes match: 10.0.0.0/16 and 0.0.0.0/0. The longest prefix (/16) wins, so the packet goes over the VPN, not out through NAT.

A call to 8.8.8.8 matches only 0.0.0.0/0, so it goes to the NAT gateway, which rewrites the private source address to its own public one. The database subnets have no default route at all, so they cannot reach the internet.

Routing only says where a packet can go; security groups say whether it may. A stateful security group on the database allows port 5432 from the app tier only. A stateless network ACL on the subnet is a coarse backstop. 7 free /20s remain for growth, and IPv6 would give each subnet a /64 with no NAT.
